preamble: Lowering of the open-mid back rounded vowel [ɔ] to the open back rounded [ɒ]. In southern England the short Middle English /ɔ/ of dog, god and fox was lowered to /ɒ/ during the 16th century, giving the LOT vowel that traditional Received Pronunciation keeps (/dɒɡ/, /ɡɒd/, /fɒks/). General American later unrounded it to /ɑ/, and present-day Standard Southern British has raised it again towards [ɔ]. In Standard Canadian English the cot–caught merger brought the THOUGHT vowel /ɔ/ together with LOT towards [ɒ], so that caught and cot are homophones.

languageExamples.language: Middle English to Early Modern English (southern England)

examples.note: Late Middle English (around 1400) had short /ɔ/ in dog and god; by 1600 it had been lowered to /ɒ/. The long /ɔː/ of boat was raised instead, to /oː/, in the Great Vowel Shift.

examples.from: caught, THOUGHT vowel /ɔ/ before the merger (cf. non-merging General American /kɔt/)
hawk, THOUGHT vowel /ɔ/ before the merger (cf. non-merging General American /ˈhɔk/)
talk, THOUGHT vowel /ɔ/ before the merger (cf. non-merging General American /tɔk/)
examples.note: Standard Canadian English merges THOUGHT and LOT towards [ɒ] (Labov, Ash and Boberg 2006, cited in the Wikipedia article); Western American English merges them towards [ɑ] instead, and Maritime and Newfoundland English towards [ɑ ~ ä].
